name: Jruq / Jru'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_locator: Jacq 2001: p. 130 (ch. 3 Word Structure, §3.3 Morphological Word, §3.3.3 Reduplication); p. 33 fn. 24; p. 113 §3.2.1; pp. 116-117 §3.2.2 Minorsyllables; p. 94 §2.3.2; p. 86 fn. 39; pp. 449-450 §6.3.1.1. Jacq 2004: p. 98 §1.2. Sidwell & Jacq 2003: p. 33 §4.2 'PWB phonological word'.
catalog_quote: [Jacq 2001: 130] Partial reduplications always involve a pre-root repetition of the initial consonant plus an extra-short version of the main vowel. This creates a minorsyllable of a very marked type. This minorsyllable vowel, while unstressed, tends to be pronounced with the same quality as the main syllable vowel. This is unlike the words which normally have a phonemic minorsyllable vowel—which is consistently schwa-like in quality (§3.2.2). ... [p. 33 fn. 24] Jruq does not have word level pitch distinctions, only sentential pitch indicating phrase boundaries, focus, and interrogatives versus declaratives. ... [p. 113] More than 98% of the Jruq lexicon consists of monosyllabic words (according to Appendix I). ... [p. 117] the minorsyllables are restricted to one vowel (which is phonetically extra short in length, see §2.3.2.5) and a small set of initial consonants /p, t, k/. ... [Jacq 2004: 98] The Jru' language is a ‘typical’ West Bahnaric language in respect to its word structure and phonemic inventory. There are no phonemic tones or registers, and the word shape is typically monosyllabic ... [Sidwell & Jacq 2003: 33] Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic-a word may consist of one or one and a half syllables. In the latter case a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable, a structurally impoverished unit that is constructed from a restricted set of segments.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule is stated. Jru' words are overwhelmingly monosyllabic (>98%); the few sesquisyllabic words (C1 ə C2V(C3), <20 items, plus partial reduplications) have a phonetically extra-short, unstressed minorsyllable before the main syllable, so prominence falls on the main, i.e. final, syllable. There are no phonemic tones or registers and no word-level pitch distinctions; pitch is sentential (intonation). The fixed: final syllable reading is an inference from 'unstressed' minorsyllable + monosyllabic word, supported by Sidwell & Jacq 2003: 33 for West Bahnaric generally ('a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (words have at most one full syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Lao loanwords carrying Lao tones are excluded from the Jruq phonology (p. 86 fn. 39). Minorsyllable vowel is contrastive only before /l, r, h/ after /p, t, k/ (pp. 109, 116-118).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word, elicited citation forms (Paksong Jru', informants Lin and Toi, recordings 1999-2000). Sentence-level intonation (rising over Topic, falling over main Verb) described separately in ch. 6.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data describe Paksong Jru' (Champassak Province, Boloven Plateau; informants Lin and Toi), which Jacq calls Jruq/Jru' = Lao 'Loven/Laven' = ISO lbo, Glottolog lave1248. Sidwell & Jacq 2003 additionally profile 'Houeikong Laven' (SIL 1978 wordlist) and L-Thongkum's Tateng Jru' as sub-varieties, and treat Juk (Glottolog dialect 6046-lbo-juk) as a separate West Bahnaric language. No dialect differences in stress are reported.
